subject: Science
central_question: How do living and non-living components interact in ecosystems, and how do human activities disturb energy flow, the ozone layer and waste balance?
in_scope_units: Ecosystems and their biotic and abiotic components, including natural and human-made ecosystems.
Producers, consumers and decomposers and their interdependence.
Food chains, trophic levels, food webs and unidirectional energy flow.
The approximately ten-percent transfer of energy between trophic levels and limits on food-chain length.
Biological magnification of persistent chemicals through food chains.
Ozone formation, protection from ultraviolet radiation and depletion by chlorofluorocarbons.
Waste generation, segregation, sewage and industrial waste treatment, recycling and environment-friendly practices.
banned_topics: Detailed management of forests, wildlife, coal, petroleum and dams, which belongs to the Sustainable Management of Natural Resources chapter.
Detailed biochemical pathways of photosynthesis and respiration.
Global warming and climate-change mechanisms not discussed in this chapter.
Detailed sewage-treatment engineering or industrial process design beyond the activities in the chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: An ecosystem contains only living organisms.
known_pitfalls.correction: An ecosystem includes interacting biotic components and abiotic physical factors such as temperature, rainfall, wind, soil and minerals.

known_pitfalls.claim: Decomposers destroy nutrients and remove them from the ecosystem.
known_pitfalls.correction: Decomposers break complex organic remains into simple inorganic substances that return to the soil and can be reused by plants.

known_pitfalls.claim: Energy cycles back from consumers to producers.
known_pitfalls.correction: Energy flow is unidirectional and decreases at each trophic level; it does not return to the previous level.

known_pitfalls.claim: Ten percent of sunlight reaching Earth is captured by plants.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter states that green plants in a terrestrial ecosystem capture about 1% of the sunlight falling on their leaves, and on average about 10% of food energy becomes available to the next trophic level.
Ozone is poisonous near living organisms, but at higher atmospheric levels it protects Earth by absorbing harmful ultraviolet radiation.

known_pitfalls.claim: Biodegradable waste can never harm the environment.
known_pitfalls.correction: Even biodegradable waste can cause problems if produced or accumulated faster than natural processes can handle it.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Activities 13.1-13.2 to classify ecosystem components and build an aquatic food chain.
Use the food-chain figures and Exercises Q4-Q6 to analyse trophic levels, energy transfer and ecosystem disturbance.
Use NCERT Activity 13.3 and Exercise Q6 to explain pesticide entry and biological magnification.
Use NCERT Activity 13.4 and Exercise Q9 for ozone formation, CFCs and protection from UV radiation.
Use NCERT Activities 13.5-13.9 and Exercises Q1, Q3, Q7 and Q8 for waste classification and management.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The end-of-chapter EXERCISES contain Questions 1-9 on biodegradability, food chains, environment-friendly practices, trophic-level disturbance, biological magnification, waste and ozone depletion.
